Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- Humza Ismail hasn't spent much time in Raleigh, North Carolina, since he started graduate school two years ago. But when he heard two former acquaintances were arrested on terrorism charges this week, he says, "Honestly, I wasn't surprised." Omar Aly Hassan, left, and Ziyad Yaghi were clear on where they stood on terrorism, an acquaintance said. Omar Aly Hassan, Ziyad Yaghi and five others are charged with conspiring to commit violent jihad overseas. An eighth suspect is still being sought, authorities have said. When he lived in Raleigh, Ismail worshipped at the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. When groups of young men talked there, Ismail says, the conversation often turned to religion and politics, and Hassan and Yaghi made it clear where they stood. "When it came to something like suicide bombing, they would say, 'If it's a benefit for the Muslims then something like that can be permissible,' " Ismail says. "I could tell it was something they wanted to do." But, he adds, "They never indicated or said 'we are going to make jihad overseas.'" Ismail says the duo spoke in glowing terms about Osama bin Laden, calling him a scholar and a mujahedeen. "You could tell they were being influenced by somebody," Ismail says. He does not know by whom. He feels they were susceptible to a message of violence "because it sounded cool and exciting." Ismail says he strenuously disagreed with Yaghi and Hassan's views on terrorism even, he says, getting into a public shouting match with them at a restaurant. He says he told them, "You can't do this, man. You can't say it is OK. "That is corruption and terrorism and that is not permissible in Islam." Ismail says he and others raised concerns about Hassan and Yaghi to officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh, but were "overlooked." "I did my part," Ismail says. Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no information about complaints concerning Hassan and Yaghi. On Saturday, however, he informed CNN that he had researched the matter and learned there was a complaint several years ago against an individual at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not have the name of that person. "It was reported to the FBI," said Aukhil. "The FBI did take note of it in their investigation." Efforts to reach attorneys representing Hassan and Yaghi were unsuccessful.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Humza Ismail has not spent much time in Raleigh, North Carolina, since beginning graduate school two years ago. But when he learned this week that two former acquaintances had been arrested on terrorism charges, he said, “Honestly, I wasn’t surprised.”

Omar Aly Hassan and Ziyad Yaghi, an acquaintance said, were clear about where they stood on terrorism. Hassan, Yaghi, and five others have been charged with conspiring to commit violent jihad overseas. Authorities have said an eighth suspect is still being sought.

When Ismail lived in Raleigh, he worshipped at the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. He said that when groups of young men gathered there, their conversations often turned to religion and politics, and Hassan and Yaghi made their views plain.

“When it came to something like suicide bombing, they would say, ‘If it’s a benefit for the Muslims then something like that can be permissible,’” Ismail said. “I could tell it was something they wanted to do.”

But he added, “They never indicated or said, ‘We are going to make jihad overseas.’”

Ismail said the two spoke admiringly of Osama bin Laden, describing him as a scholar and a mujahedeen.

“You could tell they were being influenced by somebody,” Ismail said, though he said he did not know by whom. He believed they were susceptible to a message of violence “because it sounded cool and exciting.”

Ismail said he strongly disagreed with Yaghi and Hassan’s views on terrorism, adding that he once became involved in a public shouting match with them at a restaurant. He said he told them, “You can’t do this, man. You can’t say it is OK.

“That is corruption and terrorism, and that is not permissible in Islam.”

Ismail said he and others raised concerns about Hassan and Yaghi with officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh, but that those concerns were “overlooked.”

“I did my part,” Ismail said.

Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no information about complaints concerning Hassan and Yaghi. On Saturday, however, he told CNN that he had researched the matter and learned there had been a complaint several years ago against an individual at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not have that person’s name.

“It was reported to the FBI,” Aukhil said. “The FBI did take note of it in their investigation.”

Efforts to reach attorneys representing Hassan and Yaghi were unsuccessful.

Still, when he learned this week that two men he once knew had been arrested on terrorism-related charges, he said his reaction was not shock. “Honestly, I wasn’t surprised,” he said.

According to an acquaintance, Omar Aly Hassan and Ziyad Yaghi had made their views on terrorism apparent. Hassan, Yaghi, and five other people have been accused of plotting to carry out violent jihad abroad. Authorities have said an eighth suspect remains at large.

While living in Raleigh, Ismail attended the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. He said that when groups of young men gathered there, their discussions frequently shifted toward religion and politics, and that Hassan and Yaghi left little doubt about their positions.

Ismail recalled that on subjects such as suicide bombings, they would argue that “if it’s a benefit for the Muslims,” such actions could be allowed. He said he sensed that this was something they were interested in doing. However, he added that they never directly stated that they intended to go overseas to wage jihad.

Ismail said the two men praised Osama bin Laden, describing him as both a scholar and a mujahedeen. He believed they were being shaped by someone’s influence, though he said he did not know whose. In his view, they were open to violent ideas because such ideas seemed “cool and exciting” to them.

Ismail said he strongly opposed Yaghi and Hassan’s beliefs about terrorism, and that at one point he even argued with them loudly in public at a restaurant. He said he told them they could not justify such actions and that calling them acceptable was wrong. He described terrorism as corruption and said it is not permitted in Islam.

According to Ismail, he and others alerted leaders at the Islamic Center of Raleigh about their concerns regarding Hassan and Yaghi, but those concerns were “overlooked.” “I did my part,” he said.

Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no knowledge of complaints involving Hassan and Yaghi. By Saturday, however, he told CNN he had looked into the issue and found that a complaint had been made several years earlier about someone at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not know the person’s name.

“It was reported to the FBI,” Aukhil said, adding that the FBI included it in its investigation.

Attempts to contact lawyers for Hassan and Yaghi were not successful.
